cards.front: Many type II restriction sites are {{c1::palindromes}} of four to eight base pairs.
cards.back: They read the same 5' to 3' on both strands.
cards.quote: Many sites are palindromes of four to eight base pairs: they read the same 5' to 3' on both strands.
cards.section: Cut at a known site, then seal the join

cards.front: EcoRI recognizes 5'-GAATTC-3' and cuts each strand between G and A. What kind of ends result, and why can they pair?
cards.back: Single-stranded 5' AATT overhangs, because the cuts sit four bases apart. The complementary overhangs let EcoRI ends pair, so they are called sticky.
cards.quote: The cuts sit four bases apart, leaving single-stranded 5' AATT overhangs that let EcoRI ends pair, so they are called sticky, or cohesive.
cards.section: Cut at a known site, then seal the join

cards.front: What kind of ends does SmaI leave at CCCGGG?
cards.back: Blunt ends, because it cuts both strands at the same point.
cards.quote: SmaI cuts both strands at the same point in CCCGGG and leaves blunt ends.
cards.section: Cut at a known site, then seal the join

cards.front: EcoRI leaves AATT overhangs and BamHI leaves GATC overhangs. Will an EcoRI-cut insert pair with a BamHI-cut vector end?
cards.back: No. Sticky means single-stranded, not universally compatible, and AATT and GATC do not pair. Using EcoRI at one end and BamHI at the other also fixes the insert's orientation.
cards.quote: For enzymes like these, which leave a fixed overhang, the same enzyme on vector and insert gives compatible ends
cards.section: Cut at a known site, then seal the join

cards.front: What bond does DNA ligase form to seal a join between cut ends?
cards.back: The missing phosphodiester bond between a 3'-OH and a 5'-phosphate on each strand.
cards.quote: DNA ligase forms the missing phosphodiester bond between a 3'-OH and a 5'-phosphate on each strand.
cards.section: Cut at a known site, then seal the join

cards.front: A cloning vector carries an origin of replication, a selectable marker and a cloning site. What does each do?
cards.back: The origin lets the host copy the plasmid so daughter cells keep it. The marker, such as ampicillin resistance, selects cells that hold it. The cloning site of unique restriction sites takes the insert.
cards.quote: A cloning vector carries an origin of replication, without which the plasmid is lost as cells divide; a selectable marker such as ampicillin resistance; and a cloning site of unique restriction sites.
cards.section: Into bacteria: retain, screen, confirm

cards.front: What is transformation in bacteria, and how is it different from transfection?
cards.back: Transformation is bacterial uptake of naked DNA, for example after cold CaCl2 and heat shock or electroporation. Transfection is DNA entry into animal cells.
cards.quote: Bacterial uptake of naked DNA is transformation: cold calcium chloride and a brief heat shock, or an electric pulse (electroporation), let a fraction of cells take it up.
cards.section: Into bacteria: retain, screen, confirm

cards.front: In cloning, ampicillin selection kills plasmid-free cells. Why is a second step, screening, still needed?
cards.back: Ampicillin spares any cell with a plasmid, including cells with an empty vector. Screening asks which plasmid survived, that is, whether it carries the insert.
cards.quote: Selection on ampicillin kills plasmid-free cells but spares empty vectors, so screening asks which plasmid survived.
cards.section: Into bacteria: retain, screen, confirm

cards.front: In blue-white screening with the cloning site inside lacZ-alpha, why do recombinant colonies usually stay white on X-gal?
cards.back: An insert usually disrupts lacZ-alpha, so no working beta-galactosidase forms and X-gal stays colorless. White is a strong hint, not proof: some white colonies carry no insert.
cards.quote: An insert usually disrupts lacZ-alpha, so recombinant colonies stay white, but some white colonies carry no insert.
cards.section: Into bacteria: retain, screen, confirm

cards.front: On an ampicillin plate with X-gal, a colony from a lacZ-alpha cloning is blue. What does it most likely carry?
cards.back: A vector that closed up without an insert, leaving lacZ-alpha intact, so the enzyme works and X-gal turns blue.
cards.quote: A vector that closed up without an insert, leaving lacZ-alpha intact.
cards.section: Into bacteria: retain, screen, confirm

cards.front: What four ingredients does a PCR need?
cards.back: A template, two primers, four dNTPs and a DNA polymerase.
cards.quote: PCR needs a template, two primers, four dNTPs (see nucleotide metabolism) and a DNA polymerase
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: Name the three steps of a PCR cycle in order, with the temperature of the first and of extension with Taq.
cards.back: Denature (about 94 to 98 C), anneal (a few degrees below the primers' melting temperature), extend (typically 72 C for Taq).
cards.quote: Denature at about 94 to 98 °C to separate the strands.
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: Why must a PCR primer pair bind opposite strands with their 3' ends pointing toward each other?
cards.back: Polymerase adds nucleotides only to a primer's 3'-OH, so inward-facing 3' ends extend across the region the primers bound.
cards.quote: which adds nucleotides only to the 3'-OH of a primer paired with a template, as in DNA replication
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: Primers are commonly {{c1::15 to 30}} nucleotides, with matched melting temperatures and no self-pairing or hairpins.
cards.quote: Primers are commonly 15 to 30 nucleotides, with matched melting temperatures and no self-pairing or hairpins.
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: After two ideal PCR cycles from one long genomic duplex, are any double-stranded molecules bounded by both primers?
cards.back: No. First copies start at one primer but run past the other site. Exact-length strands appear in cycle 2, still paired with longer strands; exact-length duplexes first appear in cycle 3.
cards.quote: Exact-length strands appear in cycle 2, paired with longer strands; exact-length duplexes first appear in cycle 3.
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: One long genomic duplex is the template. With ideal copying, how many exact-length duplexes exist after 4 cycles?
cards.back: 8. Exact-length duplexes number 2^n - 2n per starting duplex: 2^4 - 2(4) = 16 - 8 = 8.
cards.quote: After n ideal cycles, exact-length duplexes number 2^n - 2n per starting genomic duplex.
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: A PCR starts from 5 double-stranded template molecules and doubles perfectly every cycle. How many copies exist after 20 cycles?
cards.quote: N = N0 x (1 + E)^n, with E = 1 for perfect doubling
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: Why does making more DNA by PCR neither identify nor quantify the starting amount?
cards.back: Amplification is exponential only early. Reactions with different starting amounts can converge on the same plateau, and primers and sites set what is copied, not what the product is.
cards.quote: Amplification is exponential only early; in one model system, reactions with different starting amounts converged on the same plateau.
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: What is the threshold cycle (Ct) in real-time PCR?
cards.back: The cycle at which fluorescence crosses a set threshold during exponential amplification.
cards.quote: is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a set threshold during exponential amplification
cards.section: Counting from when the signal appears

cards.front: How does RT-PCR differ from real-time quantitative PCR, and what does RT-qPCR measure?
cards.back: RT-PCR first copies RNA into cDNA. qPCR reads fluorescence each cycle. RT-qPCR combines the two to measure mRNA.
cards.quote: RT-PCR (reverse-transcription PCR) first copies RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA); RT-qPCR combines them to measure mRNA.
cards.section: Counting from when the signal appears

cards.front: With matched, near-perfect efficiency and the same threshold, what does a lower Ct mean, and what does one cycle earlier mean at 100% efficiency?
cards.back: A lower Ct means more starting template. One cycle earlier means twice the starting template.
cards.quote: a lower Ct means more starting template; at 100% efficiency, one cycle earlier means twice the starting template.
cards.section: Counting from when the signal appears

cards.front: In relative qPCR, target and reference Ct values both move one cycle earlier in a treated sample. Has target abundance changed relative to the reference?
cards.back: No. Subtracting reference Ct from target Ct removes the shared shift, so delta Ct is unchanged. Relative qPCR asks whether that gap changes between conditions.
cards.quote: Subtracting reference Ct from target Ct removes the shared shift, so delta Ct is unchanged
cards.section: Counting from when the signal appears

cards.front: Both qPCR assays are about 100% efficient and the reference gene does not change. Target Ct is 28.0 in treated and 25.0 in control cells; reference Ct is 18.0 in treated and 17.0 in control. What is the fold change in treated cells?
cards.back: dCt treated = 28.0 - 18.0 = 10.0; dCt control = 25.0 - 17.0 = 8.0; ddCt = +2.0. Fold change = 2^-2 = 0.25, so target mRNA is about 4-fold lower in treated cells.
cards.quote: fold change = 2^(-ΔΔCt), where ΔCt = Ct(target) - Ct(reference)
cards.section: Counting from when the signal appears

cards.front: What two assumptions does the delta delta Ct fold-change method make?
cards.back: Equal efficiencies near 100% for both assays, and a reference gene shown not to change in this experiment.
cards.quote: The method assumes equal efficiencies near 100% for both assays and a reference gene shown not to change in this experiment.
cards.section: Counting from when the signal appears

cards.front: In an agarose gel, which way does DNA move, and which fragments move faster?
cards.back: Toward the positive electrode, because of its negatively charged backbone. Smaller linear fragments move faster through the mesh.
cards.quote: DNA's negatively charged backbone moves toward the positive electrode, and smaller linear fragments move faster through the mesh.
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: A PCR gives a single band of the expected size. What can you conclude, and what readout adds identity?
cards.back: Only size: a right-sized band is evidence about size, not identity. A blot adds identity, since a labeled probe lights up only complementary fragments.
cards.quote: A right-sized band is evidence about size, not identity.
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: Which molecule does each blot detect: Southern, Northern, Western?
cards.back: Southern: DNA, with a labeled probe. Northern: RNA, with a probe. Western: protein, separated by SDS-PAGE and detected with an antibody.
cards.quote: A Western blot transfers proteins separated by SDS-PAGE and detects one with an antibody
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: Which failure does each control detect: no-template control and no-RT control?
cards.back: No-template: PCR contamination. No-RT: genomic DNA in an RNA preparation.
cards.quote: a no-template control detects PCR contamination, and a no-RT control detects genomic DNA in an RNA preparation
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: What do a positive control and a spike-in inhibitor check each tell you about a negative result?
cards.back: A positive control shows the assay works. A spike-in shows a negative sample means the target was not detected, rather than the reaction failing.
cards.quote: a positive control shows the assay works, and an inhibitor check such as a spike-in shows that a negative sample means the target was not detected rather than that the reaction failed;
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: In an RT-qPCR run, the no-RT control crosses the threshold ten cycles after the matched full reaction at about equal efficiency. Does genomic DNA explain much of the signal?
cards.back: Very little. Ten cycles later means about 2^10, roughly 1,000-fold, less template: about a tenth of a percent of the signal.
cards.quote: At about equal efficiency, ten cycles later means about 2^10, or roughly 1,000-fold, less template: about a tenth of a percent of the signal.
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: In RT-qPCR from cultured-cell RNA, the full reaction has Ct 24 and the matched no-RT reaction has Ct 25. Efficiencies are about equal. How much of the main signal may be genomic DNA?
cards.back: About half. With no cDNA made, the no-RT signal comes from DNA already in the RNA. One cycle later means about half the template.
cards.quote: With no cDNA made, that signal comes from DNA already in the RNA.
cards.section: Reading the result: size, identity and controls

cards.front: A 5.0 kb vector and a 1.2 kb insert are cut with EcoRI and BamHI, ligated, transformed and selected on ampicillin. Insert plus vector gives 200 colonies; vector alone with ligase gives 180. Interpret this.
cards.back: Most colonies probably lack the insert. A vector cut by both enzymes cannot close on itself, so vector-only colonies come from singly cut vector that re-ligates, or uncut plasmid. That background is 180 of 200.
cards.quote: You cut a 5.0 kb vector and a 1.2 kb insert with EcoRI and BamHI, ligate, transform and select on ampicillin.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: To cut the background in a two-enzyme cloning, you dephosphorylate the cut vector with alkaline phosphatase. Why does this reduce vector-only colonies but still allow insert colonies?
cards.back: Without 5'-phosphates the vector cannot re-ligate to itself. The insert still supplies phosphates for each junction, so vector-insert joins can form.
cards.quote: Without 5'-phosphates it cannot re-ligate, while the insert still supplies phosphates for each junction.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After redesign, how do you screen colonies for the insert, and what bands should an EcoRI plus BamHI digest give?
cards.back: Colony PCR or an EcoRI plus BamHI digest, expecting bands of 5.0 and 1.2 kb, then sequencing across both junctions and through the insert.
cards.quote: Screen colonies by colony PCR or by EcoRI plus BamHI digest, expecting bands of 5.0 and 1.2 kb
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A cloning uses only EcoRI on both vector and insert. Using the rules for compatible ends, predict two problems.
cards.back: The insert can ligate in either orientation, since both ends match. The cut vector's own EcoRI ends can also re-close without an insert. Two different enzymes with non-pairing ends fix orientation.
cards.quote: two enzymes whose ends are distinct and cannot pair, such as EcoRI at one end and BamHI at the other, also fix the insert's orientation.
cards.section: Cut at a known site, then seal the join

cards.front: Two cDNA samples are amplified for 40 cycles and give equally bright bands of the expected size. Real-time runs at equal efficiencies near 100% give Ct 20 for A and 26 for B. Reconcile the two results.
cards.back: Sample A started with about 2^6, or 64, times more target. By 40 cycles reactions can reach a plateau (the lesson shows convergence in one model system), so band brightness need not reflect starting amount; Ct, taken during exponential amplification, does.
cards.quote: Amplification is exponential only early; in one model system, reactions with different starting amounts converged on the same plateau.
cards.section: PCR: copying one bounded region

cards.front: Why does Taq polymerase give more copying errors than Pfu, and why were early PCRs unable to use a single enzyme addition?
cards.back: Taq lacks a 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease. The first PCR used Klenow fragment, which heating destroyed, so fresh enzyme was added every cycle; Taq survives denaturation.
cards.quote: Taq lacks a 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease, so its copies carry more errors.
cards.section: Why PCR no longer needs fresh enzyme each cycle
